title: Pelvis & Perineum
summary: Explore the bony pelvis, pelvic floor, urinary and reproductive organs, and the vessels and nerves of the perineum.

lessons.title: Bony Pelvis and the Pelvic Floor (Levator Ani)

levels.kid:
Your pelvis is a big ring of bone at the bottom of your belly. It looks a bit like a bowl. You can feel the top edges as your hip bones when you put your hands on your hips.

This bony bowl does two jobs. It carries the weight of your upper body down to your legs. It also protects soft parts inside, like your bladder.

But a bowl with no bottom would let things fall out! So the bottom is closed by a stretchy sheet of muscle called the **pelvic floor**. It works like a trampoline or a hammock. When you cough or jump, it squeezes up to hold everything in place. It also helps you hold in pee until you reach the bathroom.
levels.hs:
The **bony pelvis** is a ring made of the two **hip bones** (each formed from three fused bones: the **ilium**, **ischium** and **pubis**), the **sacrum** and the **coccyx** (tailbone). In front, the two pubic bones meet at a cartilage joint called the **pubic symphysis**. At the back, each ilium joins the sacrum at a **sacroiliac joint**.

The pelvis has two parts:
- The **greater (false) pelvis** sits above the **pelvic brim** and is really part of the abdomen.
- The **lesser (true) pelvis** lies below the brim and holds the bladder, rectum and reproductive organs.

The opening at the brim is the **pelvic inlet**. The lower opening is the **pelvic outlet**.

The outlet is closed by the **pelvic diaphragm**, a funnel of muscle made mostly of the **levator ani** plus a small muscle called the coccygeus. The levator ani supports the organs, resists pressure when you cough or lift, and helps control urine and stool. Its innermost part, the **puborectalis**, loops around the rectum like a sling and pulls it forward, which helps keep stool in.

Real example: male and female pelves differ. The female pelvis usually has a wider, more oval inlet and a wider **subpubic angle** (roughly 80 to 90 degrees or more, compared with roughly 50 to 60 degrees in males), adaptations for childbirth.
levels.college:
**Bones and joints.** Each hip bone (os coxae) forms when the ilium, ischium and pubis fuse at the **acetabulum**, usually by the late teens. The posterior ring is the sacrum (five fused vertebrae) and coccyx. Stability depends far more on ligaments than on bony fit:
- **Sacroiliac joints**: partly synovial and partly fibrous, held by strong interosseous and posterior sacroiliac ligaments.
- **Sacrospinous** (sacrum to ischial spine) and **sacrotuberous** (sacrum to ischial tuberosity) ligaments turn the sciatic notches into the **greater and lesser sciatic foramina**. They also resist the sacrum tipping forward under body weight.
- **Pubic symphysis**: a secondary cartilaginous joint with a fibrocartilage disc.

**Landmarks.** The **pelvic brim (linea terminalis)** runs from the sacral promontory along the arcuate line and pectineal line to the pubic crest. The outlet is diamond-shaped, bounded by the pubic arch, ischial tuberosities, sacrotuberous ligaments and coccyx.

**Pelvic diaphragm.** The floor is made of the levator ani plus coccygeus (ischiococcygeus). The levator ani has three parts:
- **Pubococcygeus**: pubis to coccyx and the anococcygeal body.
- **Puborectalis**: a U-shaped sling around the anorectal junction that creates the anorectal angle.
- **Iliococcygeus**: arises from the **tendinous arch of levator ani**, a thickening of obturator internus fascia.

The **urogenital hiatus** in front lets the urethra (and vagina) pass. The rectum passes behind it.

**Innervation.** The levator ani is supplied mainly by the **nerve to levator ani** (from S3 to S4) on its pelvic surface. The pudendal nerve's contribution is debated.

**Function.** The floor keeps tonic resting tone. It contracts reflexively when abdominal pressure rises, as in coughing, and relaxes during voiding and defecation. Paradoxical contraction during straining is a recognised cause of constipation.
levels.phd:
**Ring mechanics.** The pelvis is a closed ring, so a single break is uncommon: disruption at one point usually implies a second injury elsewhere in the ring, whether bony or ligamentous. Weight passes from the sacrum through the sacroiliac joints to the acetabula when standing, and to the ischial tuberosities when sitting. **Nutation** (forward tilt of the sacral promontory) is limited by the sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments. During pregnancy, relaxin and oestrogen loosen the ligaments, increasing sacroiliac and symphyseal mobility.

**Obstetric dimensions.** The key inlet measure is the **obstetric conjugate**, from the promontory to the posterior symphysis, normally about 11 cm or more. Clinicians estimate it from the diagonal conjugate, which is roughly 1.5 to 2 cm longer. The narrowest plane is at the interspinous diameter, roughly 10 cm. The Caldwell-Moloy classification (1933) described four pelvic shapes: gynecoid, android, anthropoid and platypelloid. Real pelves form a continuum rather than four separate types, and the scheme now predicts labour outcomes poorly.

**Levator ani anatomy revisited.** MRI and dissection work by DeLancey and colleagues reclassified the levator into **pubovisceral** (pubovaginal, puboperineal and puboanal parts), puborectal and iliococcygeal portions. This scheme emphasises fibres that insert into the organs and the perineal body. Intramuscular stimulation studies (Barber and colleagues) support innervation mainly from the sacral-plexus nerve to levator ani, with the pudendal nerve supplying mainly the external sphincters.

**Support theory.** DeLancey's three levels of support pair with a muscle-ligament interaction. The levator's resting tone closes the urogenital hiatus and creates a near-horizontal **levator plate** on which the organs rest. When the muscle is damaged, connective tissue is loaded continuously and gradually fails, which is the proposed path to prolapse.

**Birth injury.** Computer models (Lien and colleagues, 2004) predict that the most medial pubovisceral fibres stretch about 3.3 times their length during crowning. This is far beyond the stretch striated muscle normally tolerates and explains their tendency to tear away from the pubic bone.
levels.expert:
**Levator avulsion in practice.** 3D/4D transperineal ultrasound (Dietz) and MRI detect levator avulsion, detachment of the puborectalis/pubovisceral muscle from the inferior pubic ramus. It is reported after roughly 10 to 35% of first vaginal births, with higher rates after forceps delivery. Avulsion roughly doubles the risk of anterior and central compartment prolapse and predicts prolapse returning after repair. **Ballooning**, an excessively enlarged levator hiatus on Valsalva, is an independent risk marker. Surgically repairing avulsion has not proven useful, so prevention (choice of delivery method and avoiding forceps where possible) is the main focus of current research.

**Pelvic ring trauma.** The Young-Burgess classification sorts injuries by force: anteroposterior compression (open-book), lateral compression and vertical shear. In open-book injuries, symphyseal widening tears the sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments and the anterior sacroiliac ligaments, enlarging the pelvic volume. Bleeding comes mostly from the presacral venous plexus and cancellous bone, less often from arteries. That explains why circumferential binders centred on the greater trochanters (not the iliac crests) and preperitoneal packing can work. Angiographic embolisation is reserved for arterial bleeding.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** Sacral fractures are classified by Denis zone (1 lateral to the foramina, 2 through them, 3 medial to them). The risk of nerve injury rises sharply in zone 3, where the S2 to S4 roots can be injured, causing bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction. Spinopelvic dissociation (U- or H-type sacral fractures) needs lumbopelvic fixation. Sacral insufficiency fractures in older adults are easily missed on plain films, while MRI or CT shows the classic 'Honda sign'. Sacroiliac screw placement depends on reading sacral dysmorphism (upper sacral segments that sit too high relative to the iliac crests, with angled alae), because the safe bony corridor can be narrow.

**Open questions.** Is levator injury mainly a tear at the bony attachment or a loss of the nerve supply? Can stem-cell or tissue-engineered approaches restore muscle that has torn away from bone? How much of chronic pelvic pain comes from muscle tone that stays too high (hypertonic floor dysfunction)? Pelvic floor physical therapy is strongly supported for stress incontinence, but its value for established prolapse is more modest.

keyPoints: The hip bone forms from ilium, ischium and pubis fused at the acetabulum
The pelvic brim divides the greater (false) pelvis from the lesser (true) pelvis
Sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments create the greater and lesser sciatic foramina
The pelvic diaphragm is levator ani plus coccygeus
Puborectalis slings the anorectal junction and maintains the anorectal angle
Levator ani is supplied mainly by the nerve to levator ani (S3-S4) and can avulse in childbirth

test.q: Which three bones fuse to form each hip bone?
test.explain: The os coxae forms from the ilium, ischium and pubis, which fuse at the acetabulum. The sacrum and coccyx belong to the posterior ring, not the hip bone.

test.q: The pelvic brim separates which two regions?
test.explain: The brim (linea terminalis) divides the false (greater) pelvis above from the true (lesser) pelvis below.

test.q: Which part of the levator ani forms a U-shaped loop around the anorectal junction?
test.explain: Puborectalis pulls the anorectal junction forward, creating the anorectal angle that helps with continence.

test.q: The sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments convert the sciatic notches into:
choices: The greater and lesser sciatic foramina
test.explain: These ligaments close the notches into the greater and lesser sciatic foramina. They also limit forward tilt of the sacrum.

test.q: The iliococcygeus arises from a thickening of which muscle's fascia?
test.explain: It arises from the tendinous arch of levator ani, a thickening of obturator internus fascia.

test.q: What is the main nerve supply to the levator ani?
test.explain: The nerve to levator ani from the sacral plexus is the main supply. The pudendal nerve's role is debated and it supplies mainly the external sphincters.

test.q: Compared with the male pelvis, the female pelvis typically has:
test.explain: A wider subpubic angle and a more oval inlet are adaptations for childbirth. A heart-shaped inlet is typical of the male pelvis.

test.q: What normally happens to the pelvic floor when you cough?
choices: It relaxes to let pressure out
test.explain: The floor contracts reflexively when abdominal pressure rises. It relaxes during voiding and defecation instead.

test.q: What type of joint is the pubic symphysis?
test.explain: The symphysis is a secondary cartilaginous joint with a fibrocartilage disc. The hip joint, not the symphysis, is a ball-and-socket joint.

test.q: The pelvic diaphragm consists of the levator ani plus the ___ muscle.
test.explain: Coccygeus (ischiococcygeus) completes the pelvic diaphragm behind the levator ani.

test.q: What is the gap in the front of the levator ani that lets the urethra (and vagina) pass called?
test.explain: The urogenital hiatus lies in front of the rectum and carries the urethra and, in females, the vagina.

test.q: The ilium, ischium and pubis fuse at the cup-shaped ___.
test.explain: The acetabulum is the hip socket where all three bones meet and fuse.

kidTest.q: What shape is the pelvis a bit like?
kidTest.explain: The pelvis is a ring of bone shaped a bit like a bowl.

kidTest.q: What closes the bottom of the pelvis?
kidTest.explain: The pelvic floor is a stretchy sheet of muscle, like a hammock.

kidTest.q: What does the pelvic floor do when you cough or jump?
kidTest.explain: It squeezes up to hold everything inside in place.

kidTest.q: Which organ does the pelvis help protect?
kidTest.explain: The bladder sits inside the pelvis. The heart and brain are protected by the ribs and skull.

kidTest.q: The pelvic floor is like a stretchy h _ _ _ _ _ _ that holds things up.
kidTest.explain: Like a hammock, the pelvic floor holds things up from below.

advancedTest.q: A patient has an obvious displaced fracture of the pubic ramus. Why should a posterior ring injury be actively sought?
choices: Fractures of the pubic rami are usually caused by sacral tumours
The pubic rami share a nerve supply with the sacral plexus
Pubic fractures commonly break through to the posterior side of the acetabulum
A ring is rarely broken at one point alone, so a second disruption is likely
advancedTest.explain: Because the pelvis is a closed ring, displacement at one site usually means a second bony or ligamentous injury elsewhere, often posteriorly.

advancedTest.q: Why are binders centred on the greater trochanters, together with packing, effective in many open-book injuries?
choices: Trochanteric pressure blocks blood flow in the femoral arteries
Binders realign the sacral nerve roots and restore vascular tone
Bleeding is mostly venous and bony, so reducing pelvic volume tamponades it
Most bleeding is arterial and stops when the vessel is compressed
advancedTest.explain: Open-book injuries enlarge pelvic volume. Bleeding comes mainly from the presacral venous plexus and cancellous bone, which closing the ring tamponades. Embolisation is reserved for arterial bleeding.

advancedTest.q: Modelling predicts that medial pubovisceral fibres stretch about 3.3 times their length at crowning. What is the best clinical inference?
choices: The large stretch is harmless because the floor is purely ligamentous
These fibres exceed normal tolerated stretch and tend to detach from the pubis
Iliococcygeus is the part of levator ani most likely to avulse
Stretching mainly injures the coccygeus and spares the levator ani
advancedTest.explain: The stretch exceeds what striated muscle normally tolerates, which explains why these fibres avulse from the inferior pubic ramus.

advancedTest.q: A sacral fracture runs medial to the sacral foramina (Denis zone 3). Which deficit is most concerning?
choices: Bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction from S2-S4 roots
Loss of hip flexion from femoral nerve injury
Loss of quadriceps reflex from L4 root injury
Weak hip adduction from obturator nerve injury
advancedTest.explain: Zone 3 fractures can injure the S2-S4 roots, which control bladder, bowel and sexual function. The femoral and obturator nerves arise from L2-L4.

lessons.title: Urinary Bladder and Urethra

levels.kid:
Your body makes pee all the time in your kidneys. Two thin tubes carry it down to a stretchy bag low in your belly. That bag is your **bladder**.

The bladder is like a balloon made of muscle. When it is empty, it is small and wrinkly. As it fills, it stretches out and gets bigger.

When it is quite full, tiny messengers called nerves tell your brain, "Time to find a bathroom!" Your brain can say "wait" for a while.

At the bottom of the bladder are ring-shaped muscles that squeeze shut like a drawstring on a bag. When you are ready, they relax, the bladder squeezes, and pee flows out through a tube called the **urethra**.
levels.hs:
The **urinary bladder** is a hollow, muscular organ that stores urine. It sits in the pelvis just behind the pubic bones. Urine arrives from the kidneys through two tubes called **ureters**, and it leaves through one tube called the **urethra**.

Key parts:
- The bladder wall is mostly smooth muscle called the **detrusor**. It squeezes to empty the bladder.
- The inside is lined by a special stretchy lining called **urothelium** (transitional epithelium). It can flatten out as the bladder fills and still keep urine from leaking into the tissues.
- The **trigone** is a smooth triangle on the inside floor. Its corners are the two ureter openings and the opening of the urethra.
- **Sphincters** are ring muscles that keep the exit closed. The **internal urethral sphincter** is involuntary. The **external urethral sphincter** is skeletal muscle you control.

The urethra differs between sexes. In females it is short, about 4 cm. In males it is about 20 cm and runs through the prostate and penis.

Real example: because the female urethra is so short, bacteria reach the bladder more easily. That is why bladder infections (cystitis) are much more common in women. Doctors examine the inside of the bladder with a thin camera, a procedure called **cystoscopy**.
levels.college:
**Position and relations.** When empty, the bladder lies wholly in the lesser pelvis, posterior to the pubic symphysis and separated from it by the fat-filled **retropubic space (of Retzius)**. As it fills, it rises into the abdomen, lifting the peritoneum off the anterior abdominal wall. A distended bladder can therefore be reached suprapubically without entering the peritoneal cavity. It has an apex, a body, a fundus (base) and a neck. The apex is anchored to the umbilicus by the **median umbilical ligament** (the remnant of the urachus). Posteriorly it relates to the rectum in males, with the rectovesical pouch above. In females it relates to the uterus and vagina, with the vesicouterine pouch above.

**Interior.** The mucosa is folded (rugae) except over the **trigone**. The trigone has a different embryological origin and stays smooth. The **interureteric ridge** joins the ureteric orifices. The ureters pass obliquely through the wall, which creates a flap-valve that resists reflux as pressure rises.

**Urethra.**
- Female (~4 cm): runs anteroinferiorly and opens anterior to the vaginal orifice. The external sphincter here includes the compressor urethrae and urethrovaginal sphincter.
- Male (~18-20 cm), four parts: **preprostatic** (intramural), **prostatic** (widest; the ejaculatory ducts open here), **membranous** (shortest, least distensible, encircled by the external sphincter), and **spongy** (within the corpus spongiosum, dilating at the bulb and the navicular fossa).

**Blood supply.** The **superior vesical arteries** come from the patent umbilical artery. Inferior vesical arteries (males) or vaginal arteries (females) supply the base. Venous drainage is to the vesical venous plexus and then the internal iliac veins.

**Innervation.**
- Parasympathetic, from the **pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4)**: detrusor contraction.
- Sympathetic, from T11-L2 via the hypogastric plexuses: detrusor relaxation and closure of the internal sphincter.
- Somatic, via the **pudendal nerve**: external sphincter.
levels.phd:
**Histology and the barrier.** The urothelium is the tightest epithelium in the body. Its umbrella cells carry apical plaques of **uroplakins** (UPIa, Ib, II, IIIa) arranged as asymmetric unit membrane. Together with tight junctions and a glycosaminoglycan layer, these keep water and solute flux extremely low despite steep osmotic gradients. During filling, fusiform vesicles insert into the apical membrane, increasing surface area. The urothelium is also a sensor. Stretch releases ATP, which acts on **P2X3** receptors on afferents, along with acetylcholine and nitric oxide. This contributes to fullness signaling.

**Receptor pharmacology.** The detrusor contracts mainly through **M3** muscarinic receptors (Gq, then IP3/Ca2+, with Rho-kinase sensitization). It is far richer in M2 receptors, which oppose β-adrenergic relaxation via Gi. Relaxation during storage is mediated chiefly by **β3-adrenoceptors**. The bladder neck and prostatic urethra are rich in **α1A-adrenoceptors**. These targets explain the antimuscarinics and the β3 agonist mirabegron used in overactive bladder, and α1-blockers for outflow obstruction. Adverse effects of antimuscarinics reflect M3 receptors elsewhere (dry mouth, constipation).

**Neural control.** Afferents in the pelvic nerve run on two fiber types. **Aδ fibers** signal normal fullness. **C fibers** are normally silent but are recruited in inflammation and after spinal injury. Storage is maintained by spinal reflexes: sympathetic outflow, plus the guarding reflex via **Onuf's nucleus** (S2-S4 ventral horn), which drives the external sphincter. Voiding is a switch-like spinobulbospinal reflex coordinated by the **pontine micturition center** (Barrington's nucleus). It receives input from the periaqueductal gray, which integrates afferent information. Prefrontal and insular cortex decide whether voiding is socially appropriate. When the PMC fires, it inhibits sympathetic and Onuf outflow and excites sacral parasympathetic neurons, so the sphincter relaxes as the detrusor contracts.

**Mechanics.** Compliance is high: pressure stays low over most of filling. This comes from viscoelastic wall properties and active inhibition. Loss of compliance transmits pressure to the upper tracts and endangers the kidneys.

The classic lesion localization: suprasacral spinal lesions cause **detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia**. Sacral or cauda equina lesions cause an areflexic, overdistended bladder.
levels.expert:
**Neurogenic bladder: what the lesion level predicts.**
- Above the pons (stroke, frontal tumours, normal pressure hydrocephalus): detrusor overactivity, but sphincter coordination is preserved. The patient has urgency incontinence with low-pressure, complete voiding.
- Between the pons and the sacral cord (spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis): overactivity plus **detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia**. This produces high storage and voiding pressures, vesicoureteric reflux, hydronephrosis, and historically renal failure. Clean intermittent catheterization, introduced by Lapides in 1972, transformed survival.
- Sacral, conus or cauda equina lesions: an acontractile bladder with retention and overflow.

In neurosurgery, painless urinary retention with saddle anaesthesia is a red flag for **cauda equina syndrome**. A post-void residual on bladder ultrasound is a rapid triage tool, and delayed decompression worsens bladder outcomes. Tethered cord release and spinal dysraphism surgery are routinely paired with urodynamics before and after the operation.

**Autonomic dysreflexia.** In lesions at or above T6, bladder distension can trigger massive sympathetic discharge below the lesion, causing dangerous hypertension and reflex bradycardia. The first manoeuvre is to sit the patient up and check the catheter for blockage.

**Therapies.**
- **OnabotulinumtoxinA** injected into the detrusor cleaves SNAP-25, blocking presynaptic acetylcholine release. Retention requiring self-catheterization is a key risk to counsel about.
- **Sacral neuromodulation** (S3 foramen lead) helps urgency syndromes and non-obstructive retention, although its exact mechanism remains debated (afferent modulation).
- **Percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation** is another neuromodulation option.
- Augmentation cystoplasty and Mitrofanoff appendicovesicostomy are reserved for refractory low-compliance bladders.

**Trauma and anatomical pitfalls.**
- Pelvic fracture with blood at the meatus suggests a **membranous/bulbar urethral injury**. Retrograde urethrography should precede catheter placement.
- Extraperitoneal bladder rupture often heals with catheter drainage alone. Intraperitoneal rupture, usually at the dome, needs surgical repair.

**Frontiers.**
- The "sterile urine" dogma has fallen: a resident **urinary microbiome** exists, and its role in urgency syndromes is under study.
- Anticholinergic burden has been linked to dementia risk in cohort studies, which is shifting older patients toward β3 agonists.
- Functional MRI of the PAG-insula-prefrontal network is refining models of urgency.

keyPoints: The bladder is a muscular reservoir (detrusor) lined by stretchy, impermeable urothelium
The smooth trigone lies between the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice
The female urethra is about 4 cm; the male urethra (about 20 cm) has preprostatic, prostatic, membranous and spongy parts
Parasympathetic S2-S4 fibres contract the detrusor; sympathetic fibres support storage; the pudendal nerve controls the external sphincter
The pontine micturition center coordinates detrusor contraction with sphincter relaxation
Spinal lesions above the sacral cord cause detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia; sacral lesions cause retention

test.q: The smooth muscle that forms most of the bladder wall is the:
test.explain: The detrusor muscle contracts to empty the bladder. The trigone is a region of the bladder floor, and the urothelium is its lining.

test.q: The corners of the trigone are formed by:
choices: Both ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice
The two vesical arteries and the bladder neck
Both ureteric orifices and the urachal remnant
The apex, the fundus and the bladder neck
test.explain: The trigone is the smooth triangle between the two ureteric openings and the urethral opening.

test.q: Which division of the nervous system drives detrusor contraction during voiding?
choices: Somatic fibres in the pudendal nerve
Sensory fibres in the genitofemoral nerve
test.explain: The pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4) are parasympathetic and contract the detrusor. Sympathetic fibres instead favour storage.

test.q: Which part of the male urethra is shortest and least distensible?
test.explain: The membranous urethra, surrounded by the external sphincter, is the shortest and narrowest part, and it is vulnerable in pelvic fractures.

test.q: Why are bladder infections more common in females?
choices: The female bladder lacks a trigone
The female detrusor is much thinner
The female urethra is much shorter
test.explain: A short urethra (about 4 cm) gives bacteria a short route to the bladder.

test.q: A distended bladder can be reached just above the pubis without entering the peritoneal cavity because:
choices: It is wrapped in a thick layer of visceral peritoneum
It rises and lifts the peritoneum off the abdominal wall
It sinks below the pelvic floor when it is full
It is fused to the anterior surface of the rectum
test.explain: As the bladder fills, it strips the peritoneum upward, leaving an extraperitoneal window above the pubic symphysis.

test.q: The superior vesical arteries arise from the:
test.explain: The superior vesical arteries branch from the patent proximal umbilical artery, a branch of the internal iliac.

test.q: The external urethral sphincter is controlled by the:
test.explain: The external sphincter is skeletal muscle under voluntary control through the somatic pudendal nerve.

test.q: The median umbilical ligament is the remnant of the:
test.explain: The urachus once connected the fetal bladder to the umbilicus. The umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres instead.

test.q: The fat-filled space between the pubic symphysis and the bladder is the retropubic space of ___.
test.explain: The retropubic space (cave of Retzius) lies in front of the bladder.

test.q: What is the name for looking inside the bladder with a thin camera?
test.explain: Cystoscopy passes a scope through the urethra into the bladder.

test.q: The specialized stretchy lining of the bladder is called the ___.
test.explain: Urothelium (transitional epithelium) flattens as the bladder fills while staying impermeable.

kidTest.q: What does the bladder do?
kidTest.explain: The bladder holds pee until you are ready to go.

kidTest.q: What happens to the bladder as it fills?
kidTest.explain: It is like a muscle balloon that stretches.

kidTest.q: What tells your brain the bladder is full?
kidTest.explain: Nerves carry the message to your brain.

kidTest.q: What keeps pee in until you are ready?
choices: A flap of skin over the tube
A bone that blocks the tube
kidTest.explain: Ring-shaped muscles act like a drawstring.

kidTest.q: The tube pee flows out through is the u _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The urethra carries pee out of the body.

advancedTest.q: A patient with a mid-thoracic spinal cord injury develops high bladder pressures and hydronephrosis. The best explanation is:
choices: Detrusor contraction against a sphincter that fails to relax
Destruction of Onuf's nucleus abolishing external sphincter tone
Damage to the cortex removing voluntary control over voiding timing
Loss of detrusor contraction producing an areflexic bladder
advancedTest.explain: A suprasacral lesion disconnects the pontine micturition center, so the detrusor and sphincter contract together (dyssynergia), which raises pressure. Areflexia fits sacral lesions.

advancedTest.q: Why does a β3-adrenoceptor agonist improve overactive bladder storage?
choices: It blocks α1A receptors at the bladder neck to aid emptying
It contracts the external sphincter through somatic pudendal fibres
It relaxes the detrusor through the main storage relaxation pathway
It blocks M3 receptors that drive detrusor contraction
advancedTest.explain: β3-adrenoceptors mediate detrusor relaxation during filling. Blocking M3 is how antimuscarinics work, not β3 agonists.

advancedTest.q: After a pelvic fracture, a man has blood at the urethral meatus. The safest next step is:
choices: Retrograde urethrography before any catheter is placed
Detrusor botulinum toxin injection to reduce spasm
Immediate urethral catheter placement to measure urine output
Sacral neuromodulation to restore detrusor function
advancedTest.explain: Blood at the meatus suggests membranous or bulbar urethral injury. Blind catheterization could worsen a partial tear, so imaging comes first.

advancedTest.q: A stroke in the frontal lobe causes urgency incontinence but complete low-pressure voiding. This fits because:
choices: Sympathetic outflow from T11-L2 is permanently interrupted
The sacral reflex arc is destroyed, so the bladder is areflexic
Urothelial ATP release is abolished after cortical injury
The pontine center still coordinates detrusor and sphincter
advancedTest.explain: Above the pons, cortical inhibition is lost, causing overactivity, but the intact pontine micturition center keeps the sphincter relaxing in synergy with the detrusor.

lessons.title: Male Pelvic Organs: Prostate, Seminal Vesicles and Ductus Deferens

levels.kid:
Deep in the lower belly of a boy or man, just below the bladder, sits a small gland called the **prostate**. It is about the size of a walnut. A tube that carries pee runs right through the middle of it, like a straw through a donut.

Behind the bladder are two little pouches called **seminal vesicles**. They make a sugary juice that gives sperm energy, like a sports drink for swimmers.

Sperm are made in the testicles. They travel up a long tube called the **ductus deferens**. It loops up into the belly, around the bladder, and joins the pouch's tube.

All these parts work together like a team of pipes and little factories.
levels.hs:
The male pelvis holds several organs that make and carry the fluid that sperm travel in. These are the **accessory sex glands** and their ducts.

- **Ductus deferens** (also called the **vas deferens**): a thick muscular tube about 45 cm long. It carries sperm from the epididymis next to each testis. It travels inside the **spermatic cord**, passes through the **inguinal canal**, then runs along the pelvic wall and behind the bladder. Its widened end is called the **ampulla**.
- **Seminal vesicles**: two coiled tubes, each about 5 cm long, lying behind the bladder. They make about 60-70% of semen volume, a fluid rich in **fructose** that fuels sperm.
- **Ejaculatory ducts**: each one forms where a ductus deferens joins the duct of a seminal vesicle. They pass through the prostate.
- **Prostate**: a walnut-sized gland under the bladder that surrounds the first part of the urethra, the **prostatic urethra**. It adds a thin, slightly acidic fluid that contains enzymes such as **PSA** (prostate-specific antigen).

Real example: in older men the prostate often enlarges. This is called **benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)**. Because the prostate wraps around the urethra, an enlarged gland squeezes the tube. This causes a weak urine stream and frequent trips to the bathroom, especially at night.
levels.college:
**Prostate.** A fibromuscular gland about 3 cm by 4 cm by 2 cm. Its **base** sits against the bladder neck, and its **apex** rests on the urogenital diaphragm/external urethral sphincter region. It is enclosed in a true capsule and an outer layer of pelvic fascia. Within that fascia runs the **prostatic venous plexus**, which drains to the internal iliac veins.
- **Relations:** The pubic symphysis lies in front, separated by the **retropubic space (of Retzius)**. The rectum lies behind, separated by the **rectoprostatic (Denonvilliers) fascia**. This is why the posterior surface can be felt on **digital rectal examination (DRE)**.
- **Zones (McNeal):** The **peripheral zone** makes up about 70% of glandular tissue and is where about 70% of cancers arise. The **transition zone** surrounds the urethra and is where **BPH** arises. There is also a **central zone** around the ejaculatory ducts and an **anterior fibromuscular stroma**.
- **Prostatic urethra:** The posterior wall has a ridge, the **urethral crest**, with a mound called the **seminal colliculus (verumontanum)**. The **prostatic utricle** opens on the colliculus, with an ejaculatory duct opening on each side. Many prostatic ducts open into the **prostatic sinuses** beside the crest.

**Ductus deferens.** It begins at the tail of the epididymis, ascends in the spermatic cord and enters the deep inguinal ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. It then hooks over those vessels and runs extraperitoneally on the lateral pelvic wall. It crosses **over the ureter** near the bladder ("water under the bridge"), dilates into the **ampulla**, and joins the seminal vesicle duct at the prostate base to form the **ejaculatory duct**.

**Seminal vesicles.** These lie posterolateral to the bladder base and lateral to the ampullae. Their secretion contains fructose, prostaglandins and **semenogelin** (a clotting protein).

**Supply.** Arteries come from the internal iliac system: the inferior vesical, middle rectal and the **artery to the ductus deferens**. Autonomic nerves arrive through the **inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexus**. Sympathetic fibres (from about T10-L2) drive **emission**. Parasympathetic **pelvic splanchnics (S2-S4)** stimulate secretion and erection through the **cavernous nerves**.
levels.phd:
**Developmental origins explain much of the adult anatomy.** The ductus deferens, seminal vesicles and ejaculatory ducts come from the **mesonephric (Wolffian) duct**. Their development depends on testosterone acting on the androgen receptor. The prostate, by contrast, buds from the **urogenital sinus** epithelium in response to **dihydrotestosterone (DHT)**, which **5α-reductase type 2** produces locally. Men with 5α-reductase-2 deficiency have Wolffian derivatives but a small or absent prostate. This dissociation is the rationale behind 5α-reductase inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride), which shrink the transition zone in BPH. The **prostatic utricle** is a remnant of the fused paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts, a homologue of part of the vagina and uterus.

**Zonal anatomy.** McNeal's zonal model (1968-1981) replaced the older lobar scheme. The zones differ in where they come from and what diseases they get:
- The **central zone** surrounds the ejaculatory ducts and may share Wolffian-like features. It accounts for only a small fraction of cancers.
- The **transition zone** forms the nodules of BPH, starting in periurethral tissue just above the verumontanum.
- The **peripheral zone** gives rise to most adenocarcinomas, which is why biopsy sampling targets it posterolaterally.

**Stromal-epithelial signalling.** Androgen receptor in the stroma, rather than only in the epithelium, drives prostate development, as shown in Cunha's tissue-recombination experiments. Reawakening of embryonic stromal programmes is thought to contribute to BPH.

**Smooth muscle and emission.** The ductus deferens has one of the highest muscle-to-lumen ratios in the body, with three smooth muscle layers. It contracts in response to noradrenaline and **ATP** acting on **P2X1 receptors** (co-transmission). Mice lacking P2X1 are markedly subfertile. Prostatic stromal tone is mediated largely by **α1A-adrenoceptors**, the target of uroselective blockers such as tamsulosin. Blocking α1A in the vas and seminal vesicles explains ejaculatory side effects. During emission, the **internal urethral sphincter** at the bladder neck closes under sympathetic control, preventing **retrograde ejaculation**.

**Venous drainage controversy.** The prostatic plexus communicates with the **internal vertebral (Batson) venous plexus**, which has no valves. Batson's 1940 studies proposed this route to explain why prostate cancer spreads to the lumbar spine and pelvis. Modern work suggests the bone "soil" (the RANKL/osteoblastic microenvironment) is also crucial, so the pathway is not purely mechanical.
levels.expert:
**Neurovascular bundles and the surgical planes.** In radical prostatectomy, the cavernous nerves travel in **neurovascular bundles** at about the 5 and 7 o'clock positions, outside the prostatic capsule. Walsh and Donker's 1982 cadaveric mapping made nerve-sparing surgery possible. Anatomic studies since then (Costello, Tewari) show the nerves are spread out like a curtain over the posterolateral surface rather than forming a tight cord. This has prompted intrafascial and "veil" dissections. Damage to these fibres causes **erectile dysfunction**. Damage to the external sphincter complex at the apex, or to the bladder neck, contributes to **post-prostatectomy incontinence**. The **dorsal venous complex (Santorini plexus)** anterior to the apex is the main source of bleeding and is controlled before the urethra is cut.

**Imaging-era anatomy.** **Multiparametric MRI**, read with **PI-RADS v2.1**, separates the zones by signal. The peripheral zone is judged mainly on diffusion-weighted imaging, while the transition zone is judged on T2. The PRECISION trial (2018) showed that MRI-targeted biopsy finds more clinically significant cancer than systematic TRUS biopsy, while reducing overdiagnosis. Transperineal biopsy is increasingly replacing transrectal biopsy because it largely avoids crossing the rectal wall and so carries a lower infection risk. This approach depends on understanding the perineal access route to the apex and anterior zone.

**Vas deferens in practice.** **Vasectomy** divides the vas in the scrotal spermatic cord. Recanalization and sperm granulomas are recognised pitfalls. In **inguinal hernia repair**, the external iliac vessels lie in the "triangle of doom" between the vas and testicular vessels, a danger zone for staples or tacks. Bilateral absence of the vas strongly suggests **CFTR** mutations, even without lung disease. Unilateral absence prompts checking the kidney on that side, because of their shared mesonephric origin.

**Seminal vesicle invasion** (pT3b) is a strong adverse prognostic factor and influences radiotherapy target volumes. Ejaculatory duct obstruction shows up as low-volume, fructose-negative, acidic semen. This pattern points to blocked Wolffian outflow rather than a sperm-production problem.

**Open questions.** Several issues remain unresolved:
- Why the transition zone is prone to BPH while the peripheral zone is prone to cancer.
- The role of chronic inflammation and the microbiome in prostate disease.
- Whether focal therapies such as HIFU or cryoablation can safely use zonal anatomy to spare function.

keyPoints: The prostate surrounds the prostatic urethra below the bladder; the rectum lies behind it, so it can be felt on DRE
McNeal zones: BPH arises in the transition zone, most cancers arise in the peripheral zone
The ductus deferens runs from the epididymis through the inguinal canal and crosses over the ureter to form the ampulla
Ductus deferens plus seminal vesicle duct form the ejaculatory duct, which opens on the seminal colliculus
Seminal vesicles supply most of semen volume, a fluid rich in fructose
Sympathetic nerves drive emission; parasympathetic cavernous nerves in the neurovascular bundles control erection

test.q: Which structure passes directly through the prostate gland?
test.explain: The prostatic urethra runs through the prostate. The ductus deferens joins the seminal vesicle duct at the prostate base; only the resulting ejaculatory duct traverses the gland.

test.q: Benign prostatic hyperplasia mainly arises in which zone?
test.explain: BPH nodules form in the periurethral transition zone, which is why they compress the urethra.

test.q: Why can the prostate be examined by digital rectal examination?
choices: It projects into the inguinal canal
Its back surface lies against the rectum
It lies inside the peritoneal cavity
It sits in front of the pubic symphysis
test.explain: The rectum lies directly behind the prostate, separated only by Denonvilliers fascia.

test.q: Where does the ejaculatory duct form?
test.explain: It forms where the ductus deferens joins the seminal vesicle duct at the prostate base.

test.q: Most of the volume of semen is produced by the:
test.explain: The seminal vesicles contribute roughly 60-70% of semen volume, rich in fructose.

test.q: Near the bladder, the ductus deferens relates to the ureter by:
test.explain: The ductus crosses over the ureter: 'water under the bridge.'

test.q: Most prostate cancers arise in which zone?
test.explain: About 70% of cancers arise in the peripheral zone, which is posterior and accessible to DRE.

test.q: Which nerve fibres mainly drive emission of semen?
test.explain: Sympathetic fibres (about T10-L2) contract the ducts and close the bladder neck; parasympathetic fibres mainly drive erection.

test.q: The fascia separating the prostate from the rectum is named after:
test.explain: The rectoprostatic fascia is Denonvilliers fascia. Retzius names the space in front of the bladder.

test.q: What sugar in seminal vesicle fluid fuels sperm?
test.explain: Seminal vesicle secretion is fructose-rich.

test.q: The widened end of the ductus deferens behind the bladder is called the ___.
test.explain: The ampulla joins the seminal vesicle duct to form the ejaculatory duct.

test.q: What is the common alternative name for the ductus deferens?
test.explain: Ductus deferens and vas deferens name the same tube.

kidTest.q: About how big is the prostate?
kidTest.explain: The prostate is about walnut-sized.

kidTest.q: What runs through the middle of the prostate?
kidTest.explain: The tube that carries pee goes right through it.

kidTest.q: What do the seminal vesicles make?
kidTest.explain: Their sugary fluid gives sperm energy, like a sports drink.

kidTest.q: Where is the prostate found?
kidTest.explain: It sits just below the bladder.

kidTest.q: Sperm travel up a tube called the ductus d _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The ductus deferens carries sperm from the testicle.

advancedTest.q: A man has 5α-reductase type 2 deficiency. Which pattern best fits?
choices: Normal prostate but absent seminal vesicles
Present Wolffian ducts but small prostate
Absent ductus deferens and normal prostate
Enlarged transition zone in early life
advancedTest.explain: Wolffian structures need testosterone, while the prostate needs DHT made by 5α-reductase-2.

advancedTest.q: Why do α1A-blockers for BPH often alter ejaculation?
choices: They block emission muscle in the vas
advancedTest.explain: α1A receptors also mediate smooth muscle contraction in the vas and seminal vesicles during emission.

advancedTest.q: Low-volume, acidic, fructose-negative semen most suggests:
advancedTest.explain: Absent seminal vesicle input (fructose, alkaline fluid) points to blocked Wolffian outflow, not reduced sperm production.

advancedTest.q: Unilateral absent vas should prompt imaging of the same-side kidney because:
choices: The vas drains into the renal pelvis
The ureter carries the vas blood supply
Both depend on prostate DHT signalling
advancedTest.explain: The vas comes from the mesonephric duct, which also gives rise to the ureteric bud, so their defects can occur together.

lessons.title: Female Pelvic Organs: Uterus, Ovaries and Supporting Ligaments

levels.kid:
Deep inside the lower belly, protected by the hip bones, is a small, strong organ called the **uterus**. It is shaped a bit like an upside-down pear. Later in life it is where a baby can grow.

On each side sits an **ovary**, about the size of a grape or a big almond. Ovaries hold tiny eggs and make important chemical messengers called hormones.

Thin tubes reach from the uterus toward each ovary, like arms with fingers at the ends. They catch an egg when it is released.

How does everything stay in place? Bands and sheets of tissue hold the organs, a bit like ropes and tents holding up a camp. Doctors learn these ropes carefully so they can operate safely.
levels.hs:
The female internal reproductive organs sit in the **pelvis**, between the bladder in front and the rectum behind.

- **Uterus**: a thick-walled muscular organ with a top dome (**fundus**), a **body**, and a narrow lower part, the **cervix**, which opens into the vagina. Its muscle layer is the **myometrium**; its inner lining, the **endometrium**, thickens and sheds each month during menstruation.
- **Uterine (fallopian) tubes**: run from the upper corners of the uterus toward the ovaries. Their outer ends have finger-like **fimbriae** that sweep an egg inside. Fertilization usually happens in the widest part, the **ampulla**.
- **Ovaries**: paired almond-shaped glands that release eggs (**ovulation**) and make the hormones estrogen and progesterone.

The uterus normally tips forward over the bladder. This is called **anteverted** (cervix angled forward relative to the vagina) and **anteflexed** (body bent forward on the cervix).

These organs are held in place by **ligaments**. The **broad ligament** is a sheet of peritoneum draped over the uterus and tubes like a cloth over a clothesline. The **cardinal ligaments** at the cervix give the strongest support.

Real example: in an **ectopic pregnancy**, a fertilized egg implants in the tube instead of the uterus. The tube can rupture and bleed, which is a surgical emergency.
levels.college:
**Uterus.** Its parts are the fundus, body and isthmus, plus the cervix (supravaginal and vaginal parts). The uterine cavity communicates with the cervical canal at the internal os, and the canal opens into the vagina at the external os. The wall has three layers: perimetrium (serosa), myometrium and endometrium. Its typical position is anteverted and anteflexed. Peritoneum reflects from the uterus onto the bladder, forming the **vesicouterine pouch**. Behind, it dips onto the rectum, forming the **rectouterine pouch (of Douglas)**, the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity in the upright position, where fluid or blood collects.

**Uterine tubes.** From medial to lateral: intramural part, isthmus, ampulla, infundibulum with fimbriae. The tube's lumen opens into the peritoneal cavity, so the female peritoneal cavity is not closed.

**Ovaries.** Each lies in the **ovarian fossa** on the lateral pelvic wall, bounded by the external iliac vessels and the ureter. The ovary is attached to the back of the broad ligament by the **mesovarium**.

**Ligaments and folds:**
- **Broad ligament**: double peritoneal fold with three parts: **mesometrium**, **mesosalpinx** and mesovarium.
- **Suspensory (infundibulopelvic) ligament of the ovary**: carries the ovarian vessels from the pelvic brim.
- **Ovarian ligament** and **round ligament of the uterus**: both are remnants of the embryonic gubernaculum. The round ligament passes through the deep inguinal ring and inguinal canal to the labium majus.
- **Cardinal (transverse cervical) ligaments** and **uterosacral ligaments**: condensations of endopelvic fascia that give the main passive support. The levator ani gives active support.

**Blood supply.** The **ovarian artery** arises from the abdominal aorta near L2. The **uterine artery**, a branch of the internal iliac, runs in the base of the broad ligament and crosses **above the ureter** about 1.5-2 cm lateral to the cervix ("water under the bridge"). The ovarian and uterine arteries join along the uterus. The right ovarian vein drains to the IVC; the left drains to the left renal vein.

**Lymph.** Ovarian lymph runs with the ovarian vessels to para-aortic nodes. Lymph from the cervix and body of the uterus drains mainly to internal, external iliac and sacral nodes.
levels.phd:
**Developmental logic.** The uterus, uterine tubes, cervix and upper vagina come from the **paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts**. Without anti-Müllerian hormone, the caudal parts of these ducts fuse in the midline. The septum between them is then absorbed, starting near the bottom. If fusion or septal absorption fails, the result is a didelphys, bicornuate or septate uterus. The ovaries come from gonadal ridges at upper lumbar levels and descend only into the pelvis. This explains several adult features. The ovarian artery arises near L2 and enters through the suspensory ligament. Ovarian lymph drains to para-aortic nodes. Ovarian pain is referred to T10-T11-type dermatomes, around the belly button. The gubernaculum attaches to the uterus at the uterotubal junction. That splits it into the ovarian ligament and the round ligament, which explains why the round ligament travels through the inguinal canal, just as the male gubernaculum guides the testis.

**Support as a system.** DeLancey's three-level model (1992) describes vaginal and uterine support:
- **Level I**: suspension by the cardinal-uterosacral complex to the sacrum and pelvic sidewall.
- **Level II**: lateral attachment of the mid-vagina to the arcus tendineus fasciae pelvis.
- **Level III**: fusion of the distal vagina with the perineal body and perineal membrane.

If Level I fails, the uterus or vaginal apex prolapses. If Level II fails, the bladder or rectum bulges into the vaginal wall (cystocele or rectocele). DeLancey stressed that ligaments mainly stabilize organs when the levator ani is working normally. Once the levator is injured, often by avulsion during vaginal birth, the ligaments carry loads they are poorly suited for. Histologically, the cardinal ligament is not a dense tendon. It is a perivascular sheath of loose connective tissue, smooth muscle, vessels and autonomic nerves. This is still debated in the surgical literature.

**Innervation.** Sympathetic fibres reach the organs via the superior hypogastric plexus, the hypogastric nerves and the inferior hypogastric plexus. Parasympathetic fibres come from the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4). The **pelvic pain line** separates two routes for visceral pain. Pain from structures in contact with peritoneum (fundus, body) returns with sympathetic fibres to T10-L1. Pain from subperitoneal structures (cervix, upper vagina) returns with parasympathetic fibres to S2-S4. Obstetric neuraxial analgesia targets both levels.
levels.expert:
**Ureteric danger zones.** Gynecologic surgery causes most iatrogenic ureteric injuries. The classic sites are:
- the pelvic brim, where the ureter lies just medial to the infundibulopelvic ligament as the ovarian vessels are ligated;
- the ureteric tunnel beneath the uterine artery during clamping at hysterectomy;
- the vaginal cuff and uterosacral ligament during apical suspension.

Surgeons protect the ureter by entering the retroperitoneum and identifying it on the medial leaf of the broad ligament before clamping. Endometriosis, large fibroids and cancer distort the anatomy, and preoperative ureteric stents have been used selectively in such cases. Injuries are often recognized late, so intraoperative cystoscopy after apical prolapse repair is commonly recommended.

**Nerve-sparing radical hysterectomy.** Radical (Wertheim-Meigs/Okabayashi) hysterectomy for cervical cancer removes the parametrium (cardinal ligament tissue). It can injure the inferior hypogastric plexus, leading to bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction. The Querleu-Morrow classification (types A-D) standardizes how widely the parametrium is removed. Nerve-sparing techniques keep the bladder branches of the plexus that lie in the deep, dorsal part of the parametrium. Note that the LACC trial (2018) found worse survival with minimally invasive than with open radical hysterectomy. It changed practice and showed that the surgical approach, not just the anatomy, affects cancer outcomes.

**Torsion and blood supply.** In adnexal torsion, the ovary twists on the infundibulopelvic ligament and the utero-ovarian pedicle. Because the ovary has two arterial supplies, Doppler flow may still be present even when torsion is real. Laparoscopic detorsion with ovarian preservation is now preferred, even for an ovary that looks dark, because it often recovers.

**Opportunistic salpingectomy.** Much high-grade serous "ovarian" carcinoma is now thought to begin in the fimbriae, from serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (STIC). This finding drove the practice of removing the tubes during other pelvic surgery. Its long-term effect on cancer incidence is still being studied.

**Open questions.** Several areas remain unsettled: how much mesh-based versus native-tissue apical repair is warranted, given the regulatory removal of transvaginal mesh for prolapse; how the uterosacral ligament contributes biomechanically; and the anatomy of uterus transplantation, which depends on long uterine and ovarian venous pedicles.

keyPoints: Uterus: fundus, body, cervix; usually anteverted and anteflexed
Uterine tube parts: intramural, isthmus, ampulla, infundibulum with fimbriae
Broad ligament = mesometrium, mesosalpinx, mesovarium
Cardinal and uterosacral ligaments plus levator ani give main support
Ovarian artery from aorta (via suspensory ligament); uterine artery from internal iliac
Uterine artery crosses above the ureter: 'water under the bridge'

test.q: The normal position of the adult uterus is usually:
choices: Vertical and in line with the vagina
test.explain: The uterus typically tips forward over the bladder (anteverted) and its body bends forward on the cervix (anteflexed).

test.q: Fertilization most commonly occurs in which part of the uterine tube?
test.explain: The ampulla is the widest and longest part of the tube, and it is the usual site of fertilization.

test.q: The ovarian artery usually arises from the:
test.explain: The ovaries develop at upper lumbar levels, so their artery comes straight off the aorta near L2. The uterine artery is the one that comes from the internal iliac.

test.q: Which ligament carries the ovarian vessels from the pelvic brim?
test.explain: The suspensory (infundibulopelvic) ligament carries the ovarian vessels. The ovarian ligament joins the ovary to the uterus and has no major vessels.

test.q: Near the cervix, the uterine artery relates to the ureter by:
test.explain: 'Water under the bridge': the ureter (water) passes under the uterine artery (bridge) about 1.5-2 cm lateral to the cervix.

test.q: The mesosalpinx is the part of the broad ligament related to the:
test.explain: 'Salpinx' means tube. The mesovarium is related to the ovary, and the mesometrium to the uterus.

test.q: Which structures give the main ligamentous support to the cervix?
test.explain: The cardinal and uterosacral ligaments are condensations of endopelvic fascia that anchor the cervix. The broad ligament is a peritoneal fold that gives little support.

test.q: Fluid in the peritoneal cavity of an upright woman tends to pool in the:
test.explain: The rectouterine pouch (of Douglas) is the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity in the upright position.

test.q: The round ligament of the uterus passes through the:
test.explain: The round ligament is a gubernacular remnant. It travels through the inguinal canal to end in the labium majus.

test.q: The finger-like projections at the end of the uterine tube are called ___.
test.explain: Fimbriae sweep the released egg into the tube.

test.q: What is the lower, narrow part of the uterus that opens into the vagina?
test.explain: The cervix connects the uterine cavity to the vagina through the cervical canal.

test.q: The muscular middle layer of the uterine wall is the ___.
test.explain: The three layers are perimetrium, myometrium and endometrium.

kidTest.q: What shape is the uterus a bit like?
kidTest.explain: The uterus is shaped a bit like an upside-down pear.

kidTest.q: What do the ovaries hold?
kidTest.explain: Ovaries hold eggs and make hormones.

kidTest.q: What do the tubes do with an egg?
kidTest.explain: The finger-like ends of the tubes catch the egg.

kidTest.q: What keeps the organs in place?
kidTest.explain: Ligaments act like ropes holding things steady.

kidTest.q: The organ next to the uterus that holds eggs is the o _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: There is one ovary on each side of the uterus.

advancedTest.q: Why does ovarian pain often refer to the area around the belly button rather than the pelvis?
choices: Ovarian sensory fibres travel with the round ligament to the groin
The ovary develops at lumbar levels and keeps its upper segmental supply
The pelvic splanchnic nerves project to T10 dermatomes
The ovary is innervated mainly by the pudendal nerve
advancedTest.explain: The ovary descends from an upper lumbar origin, so its visceral afferents return to about T10-T11. The pelvic splanchnic nerves are sacral, not thoracic.

advancedTest.q: A patient has a cystocele after a difficult vaginal birth but no uterine descent. In DeLancey's model this suggests failure mainly at:
choices: The suspensory ligament of the ovary
advancedTest.explain: Level II failure lets the anterior vaginal wall and bladder bulge. Level I failure would cause uterine or apical prolapse.

advancedTest.q: Doppler shows arterial flow to an ovary, yet torsion is suspected. Why should torsion not be excluded?
choices: Torsion mainly affects the round ligament vessels
The ovarian artery comes from the internal iliac
The ovary receives both ovarian and uterine arterial supply
Doppler is unreliable for ovarian venous flow
advancedTest.explain: The ovary has two arterial supplies, so flow can persist despite real torsion. The ovarian artery comes from the aorta, not the internal iliac.

advancedTest.q: Bladder dysfunction after radical hysterectomy is best explained by injury to:
choices: The round ligament within the inguinal canal
The fimbrial end of the uterine tube
The ovarian artery at the pelvic brim
Inferior hypogastric plexus fibres in the parametrium
advancedTest.explain: Removing the parametrium can cut autonomic bladder branches of the inferior hypogastric plexus. Nerve-sparing techniques aim to preserve them.

lessons.title: Perineum, Pudendal Nerve and Internal Iliac Branches

levels.kid:
Your body has a floor at the very bottom of your trunk, between your legs. Doctors call this area the **perineum**. It is shaped like a diamond.

Imagine a diamond kite drawn on the ground. Draw a line across the middle and you get two triangles. The front triangle holds the openings for pee (and, in girls, the vagina). The back triangle holds the opening for poop.

A special nerve called the **pudendal nerve** is like a phone line. It lets you feel this area and squeeze the muscles that hold in pee and poop.

A big blood pipe inside your hip, the **internal iliac artery**, splits into many smaller pipes. It is like a tree with branches that bring food and oxygen to the organs nearby.
levels.hs:
The **perineum** is the diamond-shaped region below the pelvic floor, between the thighs. Its corners are the **pubic symphysis** in front, the **coccyx** (tailbone) behind, and the two **ischial tuberosities** (sitting bones) at the sides.

A line between the ischial tuberosities divides it into two triangles:
- The **urogenital triangle** in front, containing the urethra and external genitalia (and the vaginal opening in females).
- The **anal triangle** behind, containing the anal canal and the fat-filled **ischioanal fossae** on either side.

In the middle sits the **perineal body**, a fibromuscular knot where several muscles anchor. It matters in childbirth, when it can tear.

The main nerve is the **pudendal nerve**, built from spinal nerves **S2, S3 and S4**. It carries sensation from the perineum and controls the voluntary **external urethral and anal sphincters**. That is why it is vital for continence. A memory aid: "S2, 3, 4 keeps the pee and poo off the floor."

Blood comes mainly from the **internal iliac artery**, which branches inside the pelvis to supply the bladder, rectum, reproductive organs, buttock and perineum. Its branch the **internal pudendal artery** travels with the pudendal nerve.

Real example: during childbirth, doctors may inject local anesthetic near the pudendal nerve (a **pudendal nerve block**) to numb the perineum.
levels.college:
**Boundaries and divisions.** The perineum is the space inferior to the pelvic diaphragm (levator ani and coccygeus). Its osteofibrous outline matches the pelvic outlet: pubic symphysis, ischiopubic rami, ischial tuberosities, sacrotuberous ligaments and coccyx. The interischial line splits it into urogenital and anal triangles.

**Urogenital triangle.** The **perineal membrane** is a tough sheet stretched between the ischiopubic rami. It separates:
- The **superficial perineal pouch** (below the membrane): erectile tissue (bulb, crura) with **bulbospongiosus**, **ischiocavernosus** and superficial transverse perineal muscles; greater vestibular glands in females.
- The **deep perineal pouch** (above it): external urethral sphincter, deep transverse perineal muscle (in males), and bulbourethral glands in males.

**Anal triangle.** The **ischioanal fossae** are fat-filled, wedge-shaped spaces lateral to the anal canal. They communicate behind the anus, so infection can spread from one side to the other (a "horseshoe" abscess). The **external anal sphincter** surrounds the canal.

**Pudendal nerve (S2–S4).** It leaves the pelvis through the **greater sciatic foramen** below piriformis, hooks around the **sacrospinous ligament** near the ischial spine, and re-enters through the **lesser sciatic foramen** into the **pudendal (Alcock's) canal**, a split in obturator internus fascia. Branches:
- **Inferior rectal (anal) nerve**: external anal sphincter, perianal skin.
- **Perineal nerve**: perineal muscles, external urethral sphincter, scrotal/labial skin.
- **Dorsal nerve of the penis/clitoris**: sensation.

**Internal iliac artery.** It splits near the upper border of the greater sciatic foramen into:
- **Posterior division**: iliolumbar, lateral sacral, superior gluteal.
- **Anterior division**: umbilical (gives superior vesical), obturator, inferior vesical (vaginal in females), middle rectal, uterine, internal pudendal, inferior gluteal.

The internal pudendal artery follows the nerve's course exactly, supplying the perineum.
levels.phd:
**Fascial layering and spaces.** The superficial perineal fascia (**Colles' fascia**) continues with Scarpa's fascia of the abdominal wall and the dartos layer. It attaches to the ischiopubic rami, the fascia lata just below the inguinal ligament, and the posterior edge of the perineal membrane. This explains why urine leaking from a ruptured bulbous urethra (straddle injury) spreads into the scrotum, penis and lower anterior abdominal wall but not into the thighs or anal triangle. The ischioanal fossae extend forward above the perineal membrane as **anterior recesses**, a route by which pus or blood can track.

**The deep pouch debate.** The classic picture of a flat "urogenital diaphragm", a trilaminar muscle sheet, has been largely abandoned. MRI, dissection and histology (work by Oelrich and later DeLancey) show the external urethral sphincter as a vertically extended, partly circular muscle (the **rhabdosphincter**) reaching up toward the bladder neck. In females it merges with the compressor urethrae and urethrovaginal sphincter. The deep transverse perineal muscle is weak or absent in many women, so "deep pouch" is better described as a space than as a closed compartment.

**Pudendal nerve fibre composition.** The nerve carries somatic motor axons from **Onuf's nucleus** (anterior horn of S2–S4). This nucleus is unusual: it is relatively spared in ALS but affected in multiple system atrophy, which helps explain the early sphincter EMG changes in MSA. The nerve also carries sensory afferents and sympathetic postganglionic fibres (vasomotor, sudomotor). Erectile parasympathetic fibres travel separately in the **pelvic splanchnic nerves** and cavernous nerves, not in the pudendal trunk. The pudendal nerve mediates the somatic arms of the bulbocavernosus and anal wink reflexes.

**Internal iliac variability.** The branching pattern is highly variable; Adachi's classification and its modifications describe several types based on how the gluteal and pudendal trunks arise. The obturator artery arises from the inferior epigastric in roughly a quarter to a third of people (**corona mortis** anastomosis). **Accessory pudendal arteries**, often running along the prostate, may supply much of the penile inflow.
levels.expert:
**Pudendal neuralgia and entrapment.** The **Nantes criteria** (2008) define pudendal neuralgia: pain in pudendal territory, worse with sitting, not waking the patient, with no objective sensory loss and relief from a diagnostic block. Entrapment classically occurs between the sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments (the "ligamentous clamp") or in Alcock's canal at the falciform process. Pudendal nerve terminal motor latency testing has fallen out of favour because it correlates poorly with symptoms. Image-guided blocks (CT or ultrasound at the ischial spine) are both diagnostic and therapeutic. Surgical decompression via transgluteal or transperineal routes has modest supporting evidence, including one small randomized trial.

**Obstetric relevance.** Prolonged second stage and instrumental delivery stretch the pudendal nerve, with documented denervation on EMG. Obstetric anal sphincter injuries (third/fourth-degree tears) involving the external anal sphincter and perineal body remain a leading cause of fecal incontinence in women. Endoanal ultrasound reveals occult defects that were missed clinically.

**Interventional and surgical implications.**
- **Prostate artery embolization** depends on identifying the prostatic artery, which can arise from the internal pudendal, inferior vesical or obturator arteries. Missing collaterals to the rectum or penis risks non-target embolization.
- **Postpartum hemorrhage and pelvic fracture bleeding**: internal iliac (anterior division) embolization works because of rich collaterals (lumbar, median sacral, superior rectal from the IMA). This same redundancy is why ligation lowers pulse pressure rather than stopping flow.
- Bilateral proximal internal iliac occlusion during **EVAR** can cause buttock claudication, erectile dysfunction and, rarely, colonic or spinal ischemia. This drives the use of iliac branch devices.
- Nerve-sparing radical prostatectomy protects the cavernous nerves and, when present, accessory pudendal arteries to preserve erections.

**Neuromodulation.** Sacral neuromodulation (S3) treats overactive bladder and fecal incontinence. Direct pudendal nerve stimulation is being studied as an alternative, with debate over its added benefit.

**Open questions** include the true contribution of perineal body integrity to prolapse, and individual mapping of pudendal branching (high-resolution MR neurography) to guide blocks and decompression.

keyPoints: Perineum: diamond below the pelvic diaphragm, split into urogenital and anal triangles
Perineal membrane separates the superficial and deep perineal pouches
Pudendal nerve (S2–S4) exits the greater and enters the lesser sciatic foramen into Alcock's canal
Pudendal branches: inferior rectal, perineal, dorsal nerve of penis/clitoris
Internal iliac splits into posterior (gluteal, sacral, iliolumbar) and anterior (visceral) divisions
Colles' fascia attachments explain the spread of urine after urethral rupture

test.q: Which landmarks form the lateral corners of the perineal diamond?
test.explain: The sitting bones (ischial tuberosities) mark the lateral corners. The ischial spines lie deeper and are the landmark used for a pudendal block.

test.q: The pudendal nerve arises from which spinal nerve roots?
test.explain: S2, 3, 4 form the pudendal nerve, which keeps the sphincters working.

test.q: After leaving the pelvis, the pudendal nerve re-enters the perineum through the:
test.explain: It exits via the greater sciatic foramen, hooks around the sacrospinous ligament, then enters through the lesser sciatic foramen.

test.q: Which branch of the pudendal nerve supplies the external anal sphincter?
test.explain: The inferior rectal (anal) nerve supplies the external anal sphincter and perianal skin.

test.q: Which artery belongs to the posterior division of the internal iliac?
test.explain: The posterior division gives iliolumbar, lateral sacral and superior gluteal arteries. The other choices come from the anterior division.

test.q: Bulbospongiosus and ischiocavernosus lie in which space?
test.explain: These muscles cover the erectile tissue below the perineal membrane, in the superficial pouch.

test.q: Why can an abscess on one side of the anus spread to the other side?
choices: The perineal membrane covers the anal canal
The rectum lacks a muscular wall
The pudendal canals join in the midline
Both ischioanal fossae connect behind the anus
test.explain: The ischioanal fossae communicate posteriorly, allowing a horseshoe abscess.

test.q: The artery that runs with the pudendal nerve through Alcock's canal is the:
test.explain: The internal pudendal artery, from the anterior division, follows the nerve's route to the perineum. The external pudendal arises from the femoral artery.

test.q: A line between which structures divides the perineum into two triangles?
test.explain: The interischial line separates the urogenital triangle in front from the anal triangle behind.

test.q: The pudendal nerve runs through the pudendal canal, also called ___ canal.
test.explain: Alcock's canal is a split in the obturator internus fascia.

test.q: What fibromuscular midline knot in the perineum anchors several muscles and can tear in childbirth?
test.explain: The perineal body is a key anchor of perineal support.

test.q: The tough sheet between the ischiopubic rami that separates the two perineal pouches is the perineal ___.
test.explain: The perineal membrane divides the superficial pouch from the deep pouch.

kidTest.q: What shape is the perineum?
kidTest.explain: It is diamond-shaped, like a kite.

kidTest.q: What does the pudendal nerve help you do?
kidTest.explain: It lets you feel the area and squeeze the holding muscles.

kidTest.q: The diamond splits into how many triangles?
kidTest.explain: A front triangle and a back triangle.

kidTest.q: What does the internal iliac artery carry?
kidTest.explain: It brings blood with food and oxygen to nearby organs.

kidTest.q: A nerve works like a phone l _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Nerves carry messages, like a phone line.

advancedTest.q: After a straddle injury ruptures the bulbous urethra, urine spreads into the lower abdominal wall but not the thighs. Why?
choices: Urine is drained toward the abdomen by the pudendal canal
The perineal membrane is torn and opens into the retropubic space
Colles' fascia attaches to the fascia lata just below the inguinal ligament
Scarpa's fascia ends at the pubic symphysis in the midline
advancedTest.explain: Colles' fascia is continuous with Scarpa's fascia but fused to the fascia lata, blocking the thighs while leaving a path up the abdominal wall.

advancedTest.q: Bilateral internal iliac embolization often controls pelvic bleeding without causing widespread necrosis. The best explanation is:
choices: Pelvic tissues tolerate several hours without any perfusion
Embolization occludes veins instead of the arterial branches
The pelvic organs are supplied by the external iliac artery
Collateral arteries keep perfusing the pelvic tissues
advancedTest.explain: Rich collaterals (lumbar, median sacral, superior rectal) lower pulse pressure to aid clotting while keeping tissue alive.

advancedTest.q: A patient has early external sphincter EMG denervation with parkinsonism. Which reasoning links these findings?
choices: Pudendal entrapment at the ischial spine produces parkinsonism
ALS selectively destroys Onuf's nucleus early in the disease
Multiple system atrophy affects Onuf's nucleus, unlike ALS
Pelvic splanchnic nerves carry the motor fibres to the sphincters
advancedTest.explain: Onuf's nucleus is affected in MSA but relatively spared in ALS, so early sphincter denervation points toward MSA.

advancedTest.q: A patient with perineal pain worse when sitting has normal sensation and relief after an ischial spine block. Under the Nantes criteria this supports:
advancedTest.explain: Sitting-worse pain in pudendal territory, no objective sensory loss and relief from a block fit pudendal neuralgia. Root avulsion and cauda equina usually cause sensory loss.
